title: 分布式音频与聊天
full_query: Write a technical proposal for a distributed audio streaming system. The system should include an audio streaming platform and a live chat feature. This application should be built for both browser and mobile settings. Include detailed technologies and justify why they are used. Assume the audience is a team of experienced software developers at a medium sized software company.

pointwise.title: Proposal objective and assumptions
pointwise.question: Does the proposal state its audio-and-chat product objective and the workload, performance, operating and team assumptions needed to interpret its design?

anchors.1: Neither an identifiable audio-and-chat objective nor usable design assumptions is stated.
anchors.2: Only a generic objective is given, or assumptions are listed without identifying the product they describe.
anchors.3: The product is identifiable, but an important workload, performance, operating or team assumption needed to interpret its choices is missing or too vague.
anchors.4: The objective and the assumptions needed by the design are clear, with only a minor interpretive gap.
anchors.5: The objective and necessary workload, performance, operating and team assumptions are explicit. Performance expectations are concrete enough to assess the chosen design, and team capabilities or availability relied on by the proposal are stated.

pointwise.boundary: Judge the context needed to interpret this proposal, not the ambition of its targets. Concrete expectations may be numeric or a testable behavior; no prescribed latency, uptime, team size or staffing model is required. Goals and the conditions that give them meaning remain one item. Feasibility, cost and implementation priorities are assessed separately. A missing assumption matters only when a material choice depends on it.

pointwise.title: Audio delivery path
pointwise.question: Does the proposal specify how audio reaches a playing client, including the transport and media-handling choices at the relevant handoffs?

anchors.1: No audio delivery path is specified.
anchors.2: Audio tools are named, but the proposal does not show how they move playable audio to a client.
anchors.3: Part of the path is described, but a major origin-to-player handoff or its transport/media-handling choice is unspecified.
anchors.4: The main path, component roles and transport/media-handling choices are explicit, with only a minor handoff detail missing.
anchors.5: The chosen origin, processing if used, delivery and playback form an explicit path. The proposal identifies how audio is represented or encoded and transported, and where serving, relaying or caching is handled as relevant to that path.

pointwise.boundary: Check whether the audio path and its selected technologies are described, not whether they are better than another design. No particular live/VOD model, codec, protocol, media server, cache or CDN is required. Managed handling can satisfy the item when the proposal explains what is delegated and how the client receives compatible audio. Do not require a catalogue of alternatives; reasons for choices remain PT.D1.06.

pointwise.title: Live chat delivery path
pointwise.question: Does the proposal specify how live chat messages move between participants through its chosen services?

anchors.1: No chat delivery path.
anchors.2: Only names a chat service or protocol.
anchors.3: A message path exists but a major participant/service handoff is missing.
anchors.4: Participant-to-service-to-recipient delivery and roles are clear, with a minor gap.
anchors.5: Message submission, routing to the intended conversation and recipient delivery are explicit; no specific broker, database or protocol is required.

pointwise.boundary: Check whether the report describes this required part of the system. Do not score whether its technology or architectural style is better than another.

pointwise.title: Distributed deployment responsibilities
pointwise.question: Does the proposal identify the hosting environment, implementation technologies and distributed responsibilities of its major components?

anchors.1: No usable deployment responsibilities or hosting design are given.
anchors.2: Only platform or vendor names are supplied, without component placement.
anchors.3: Some placement is described, but a central component lacks a hosting environment, implementation technology or deployment responsibility.
anchors.4: Major client, service and storage placements and technologies are clear, with a minor deployment detail missing.
anchors.5: The chosen hosting environment and major client/service/storage technologies are identified and mapped to their deployment responsibilities.

pointwise.boundary: Score specification, not vendor preference or architectural superiority. A cloud platform, managed service, self-hosted environment or justified combination is eligible. Diagrams, containers, microservices and multiple regions are not mandatory. Deployment placement is distinct from the release and maintenance practices compared in PW.D4.04.runtime/PW.D4.04.change.

pointwise.title: Browser and mobile client design
pointwise.question: Does the proposal specify browser and mobile client technologies, their audio/chat responsibilities and the client behavior needed by the chosen product?

anchors.1: Neither browser nor mobile client setting is designed.
anchors.2: One setting is missing, or both are only labels.
anchors.3: Both client settings are identifiable, but at least one lacks material technology, responsibility or product-critical behavior detail.
anchors.4: Both settings have technologies, responsibilities and the necessary client behavior specified, with one minor gap.
anchors.5: Both browser and mobile choices, audio/chat responsibilities and product-critical interaction or playback/network behavior are explicit; shared implementations clearly explain what is shared and what differs.

pointwise.boundary: Check specification for both settings, not which client technology is better. Native, cross-platform and suitable web-based routes remain eligible. A clearly specified platform with the other wholly absent scores 2; if the other exists but lacks material detail, score 3. Do not require every official UI/UX or performance example: background playback, accessibility, responsive layout, caching and state management matter here when the described product relies on them. This item does not judge whether a reason for choosing a framework is persuasive.

pointwise.question: Does the proposal explain why its major technologies are chosen for the requested audio-and-chat system?

anchors.1: No meaningful technology choices or reasons.

pointwise.title: Concrete service interfaces
pointwise.question: Does the proposal describe concrete audio-related and chat service interactions using its chosen API or messaging style?

anchors.1: No usable service interface is described.
anchors.2: An API style or messaging protocol is named, but no concrete operation or event is explained.
anchors.3: Concrete interactions are described, but a central audio-related or chat operation lacks the participants, input, result or delivery semantics needed to understand it.
anchors.4: Important audio-related and chat interactions have interpretable contracts, with only a minor input, result or delivery detail missing.
anchors.5: The chosen interface style and important audio-related and chat operations or events are explicit: who invokes or emits them, what information they carry, and what result or delivery behavior the caller/recipient expects.

pointwise.boundary: This is the level of interface detail in a technical proposal, not an implementation-ready API specification. HTTP endpoints, RPC methods, events and managed SDK operations are eligible; exact URL paths, REST, GraphQL, gRPC or WebSockets are not mandatory. PT.D1.02.audio/chat check the overall delivery path; this item checks the meaning of interactions, not the same flow arrows again. Permissions and protection are assessed in PT.D1.08.

pointwise.title: Protection of the audio-and-chat system
pointwise.question: Does the proposal specify protections for the access boundaries, sensitive data and abuse risks created by its chosen audio-and-chat design?

anchors.1: No relevant security protection is specified.
anchors.2: Security tools or slogans are listed without identifying what they protect.
anchors.3: Some protections are concrete, but a major exposure in access control, sensitive data/credentials or service abuse is left without a response.
anchors.4: The principal exposures have concrete controls and responsible components, with only a minor protection boundary unclear.
anchors.5: Controls are tied to the design's principal exposures: who may access or administer resources, how relevant data and credentials are protected, and how the service handles abuse. The responsible components and important protection limits are clear.

pointwise.boundary: Judge concrete security specification, not the number of named controls or the promise of perfect security. Public content can still need administrative access control and abuse protection; data-at-rest controls depend on what is stored. No specific authentication scheme, vault, WAF or rotation interval is required. A strong access-control description cannot earn 4 or 5 if a major sensitive-data or abuse exposure is unaddressed. Privacy obligations, content permissions and moderation decisions are compared in PW.D4.05.privacy, PW.D4.05.rights and PW.D4.05.moderation respectively, not inferred from encryption alone. v3.3: privacy, content permission and moderation plan coverage is now PT.D1.14–16; the three preserved PW children assess distinct decision usefulness.

pointwise.title: Capacity growth and traffic spikes
pointwise.question: Does the proposal specify how audio delivery, chat fan-out and shared state cope with expected growth and sudden demand?

anchors.1: No scaling or spike response.
anchors.2: Only says the system scales or names infrastructure products.
anchors.3: Some capacity response is concrete, but a major audio, chat or state bottleneck is unaddressed, or sudden spikes are ignored.
anchors.4: Main bottlenecks and growth/spike responses are specified, with a minor trigger or limit unclear.
anchors.5: The design identifies limiting resources and their capacity responses for audio, chat and shared state, including sudden demand, overload behavior and boundaries under its stated workload.

pointwise.boundary: A single managed service may cover several roles if its limits and delegated behavior are explained. No mandatory sharding, CDN, queue or multi-region route; growth and spike conditions cannot be omitted.

provenance.change_note: Restore direct scaling-plan coverage; a strong media path cannot compensate for an unaddressed chat/state bottleneck. Capacity and the behavior at its boundary are one specification.

pointwise.title: Budget and operating-resource scenarios
pointwise.question: Does the proposal explain how usage and growth affect infrastructure, maintenance and staffing costs?

anchors.1: No budget or resource implications.
anchors.2: Only calls the system cheap or gives an unexplained total.
anchors.3: Some cost drivers are concrete, but usage/growth assumptions, maintenance or staffing implications are missing.
anchors.4: Major usage-dependent and ongoing people/maintenance costs are connected to the plan, with a minor assumption gap.
anchors.5: Interpretable estimates or bounded cost-driver scenarios explain how delivery, compute/storage and maintenance/staffing burdens change with usage and growth; assumptions and unknown prices are explicit.

pointwise.boundary: No fixed low/medium/high table or current vendor quote is required. Qualitative scenarios must name what changes and why, not merely say costs rise.

provenance.change_note: Restore budget substance from PW-only coverage. Hosting cost detail without maintenance/staffing implications scores3; price precision is not a separate reward.

pointwise.title: Runtime observation and incident response
pointwise.question: Does the proposal specify useful runtime observations and how the team responds to audio/chat service problems?

anchors.1: No operating plan.
anchors.2: Only names dashboards or logging tools.
anchors.3: Some observations or actions exist, but the signal-to-diagnosis-to-response path is broken, or a major audio, chat, usage/capacity or security observation is absent.
anchors.4: Relevant observations lead to responsible diagnosis and action, with a minor signal or handoff gap.
anchors.5: Audio playback/delivery, chat operation, usage/capacity and security conditions have relevant signals, a diagnosis path and responsible incident actions; collection is proportionate to data sensitivity.

pointwise.boundary: No fixed tool, metric count or raw-chat logging. Managed observability must identify what the team sees and can do; release-specific decisions are separate.

provenance.change_note: Directly checks the runtime maintenance plan previously only compared in PW. Signals without response or response without a trigger are reciprocal3 cases.

pointwise.title: Validation and deployment-change plan
pointwise.question: Does the proposal specify how code and infrastructure changes are tested, deployed and handled if unsuccessful?

anchors.1: No change or validation plan.
anchors.2: Only names CI/CD or an automation product.
anchors.3: A pipeline is described but suitable automated/system validation, release criteria, reproducible deployment or failed-change handling has a material gap.
anchors.4: Tests, reproducible deployment and failed-change response form a clear path, with minor responsibility detail missing.
anchors.5: The plan links suitable automated checks and system/load validation to release criteria, repeatable code/infrastructure deployment and a defined failed-change response.

pointwise.boundary: No mandatory IaC product, Kubernetes or rollback technique. Roll-forward or reverting a managed configuration may be appropriate; explain the actual path. Runtime incidents not caused by changes are separate.

provenance.change_note: Restore DevOps and automated validation content. Fast deployment with no validation or failure response scores3; these are one conditional change path.

pointwise.title: Delivery sequence and team feasibility
pointwise.question: Does the proposal give a milestone sequence and a feasible delivery approach for the assumed team?

anchors.1: No delivery approach.
anchors.2: Only gives dates or names Agile/Scrum.
anchors.3: Milestones exist, but timing/effort, dependencies or the team's ability to execute them is unclear.
anchors.4: Milestone sequence, indicative effort/timing and team responsibilities are plausible and explicit, with a minor dependency gap.
anchors.5: The proposal explains what is built and validated in sequence, indicative effort or timing, dependencies and feedback/replanning points, justified by the team's available skills and capacity.

pointwise.boundary: No fixed calendar or named methodology. Ranges with explicit uncertainty are acceptable; an unordered feature list is not a delivery plan.

provenance.change_note: Restore timeline/model substance without forcing a methodology name; milestones without feasibility are3, and delivery model is judged through actual feedback and sequencing.

pointwise.title: Personal-data obligations
pointwise.question: Does the proposal address personal-data handling and the privacy context relevant to its users and deployment?

anchors.1: No privacy handling.
anchors.2: Only asserts compliance or mentions a statute.
anchors.3: Data or obligations are identified, but a consequential collection, retention, access or jurisdiction uncertainty has no response.
anchors.4: Relevant personal-data handling and obligations/assumptions are clear, with a minor unresolved detail.
anchors.5: The proposal connects personal data collected and retained to purpose, access/deletion handling and relevant jurisdiction assumptions; consequential unknown obligations have a concrete resolution step.

pointwise.boundary: No mandatory GDPR/CCPA jurisdiction. Encryption alone does not answer purpose, retention or user-data obligations; this is plan content, not legal certification.

provenance.change_note: Restore privacy coverage separately from rights and moderation. Data inventory without response to a relevant obligation is3.

pointwise.title: Audio-use permission handling
pointwise.question: Does the proposal specify how the chosen audio content is authorized and how uncertain permissions are handled?

anchors.1: No audio-use permission consideration.
anchors.2: Only says copyright does not apply or licensing will be handled.
anchors.3: Identifies a content source but not who authorizes its use or what happens if permission is absent.
anchors.4: Content model, authorization and unresolved-permission response are clear, with a minor responsibility gap.
anchors.5: For the chosen content model, the proposal identifies permission authority, how permission is established and who prevents or resolves unauthorized use.

pointwise.boundary: Original user audio is eligible; commercial music licences are not compulsory. A named content model is not proof of permission.

provenance.change_note: Restore independent content-rights scope; strong privacy cannot hide absent permission handling.

pointwise.title: Accountable chat-content handling
pointwise.question: Does the proposal define how chat-content problems are reported or detected and resolved under a responsible policy process?

anchors.1: No moderation plan.
anchors.2: Only promises moderation or names a filter.
anchors.3: A rule, detector or moderator is named, but reporting/detection, responsibility or action is missing.
anchors.4: A chat-content problem has a clear responsible action path, with a minor escalation detail unclear.
anchors.5: The proposal states relevant content-policy boundaries and links detection/reporting to accountable review or automated decisions, actions and handling of contested or escalated cases.

pointwise.boundary: No mandatory moderation vendor, all-human team or public-chat model. Closed chat still needs a proportionate responsibility path; rate limiting alone is service-abuse protection.

provenance.change_note: Restore direct moderation coverage without merging legal domains. Detection with no responsible action scores3.
